goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Cannot manage a precision measurement programme without baseline data on every instrument. Starting with pendulum_lab as primary reference standard—period measurements are reproducible, independent of operator skill, and essential for validating all subsequent work. Twelve trials will establish initial mean and variance, giving me something concrete to anchor against tomorrow's civic ledger readings. This is foundational work, not hypothesis-testing.

Day 2 continuation of baseline establishment. pendulum_lab has only 18 trials so far; the protocol requires days 1–10 of data to establish a robust baseline. I need at least 60 trials (10 days × 6 trials/day is typical cadence) to detect drift reliably and to have sufficient n for replication claims. Running 12 more trials today brings me to 30 total, which is still well short of the 60-trial target. The mean (1.6698 beats) and scatter (range 1.6527–1.6924, σ ≈ 0.012) look consistent with instrumental noise, no anomalies yet. No reason to deviate from the baseline protocol.

resonator_lab has only 12 baseline trials (days 1–2) and needs n=36 to establish a robust baseline per protocol. pendulum_lab is at 36 trials and approaching completion of the baseline phase. The resonator instruments show poor cross-correlation with pendulums (0.091 and 0.284), which is expected for independent instruments, but I need sufficient resonator_lab data before I can assess drift or detect any systematic deviations. Continuing systematic baseline accumulation on the instrument furthest from target sample size is the methodical priority.

resonator_lab has completed its baseline phase (n=30, days 1–3) with mean 2.7057 cycles/beat. Day 4 marks the transition to post-baseline monitoring. Continuing the measurement series will: (1) establish drift detection capability by accumulating post-baseline data; (2) test reproducibility of the baseline mean under identical conditions; (3) maintain instrument calibration status. The cross-check correlations are all within or near chance levels—no anomalies yet warrant investigation. Methodical continuation of the standard protocol is the appropriate next step.

Day 5: continuing baseline establishment (need n=60+ for robust 10-day baseline per protocol). resonator_lab shows tight clustering (mean 2.7004, all 48 trials within ±0.03) with no drift signal yet. All cross-instrument correlations are sub-threshold noise. No anomalies warrant deviation from schedule. Fresh measurements will improve drift detectability and baseline precision before Day 10 transition to post-baseline monitoring.

resonator_lab has completed 66 baseline trials (days 1–5) with mean 2.7027 cycles/beat and tight value spacing (0.000100 minimum). We are at day 6, transitioning out of the baseline window (days 1–10). Running 12 fresh trials will allow me to establish post-baseline characterization and begin detecting any drift. The resonator_lab shows the most complete baseline dataset and is my most frequently measured instrument. Cross-checks reveal weak correlations with other instruments (all within or near chance), but internal autocorrelation is also weak—suggesting independent behavior worth tracking precisely. This is routine maintenance of the calibration programme.

Day 7 continues the baseline period (days 1–10). resonator_lab has 84 trials; I need 96 total for a robust 10-day baseline (n≈10/day). The recent trial sequence (75–84) shows normal scatter around mean 2.7034 with no obvious drift or anomaly. Six more trials will advance toward the target while maintaining daily measurement cadence. This is routine baseline work; no evidence yet warrants deviation from the calibration protocol.

Day 8 of baseline establishment (days 1–10). resonator_lab has 96 trials accumulated; need 4 more to reach n=100 for solid baseline statistics. Yesterday's trials 91–96 show expected scatter (mean 2.7231, consistent with running baseline of 2.7050). These 6 new trials will complete a clean set of 102 readings, sufficient to detect any genuine drift post-day-10. Resonator instruments are showing modest but non-chance cross-correlations with pendulum instruments at various offsets; maintaining high-frequency measurement density now ensures I can distinguish real correlation structure from noise once baseline is closed.

Day 9 of baseline establishment (target: days 1-10). resonator_lab is at 108/target ~120 trials for robust baseline statistics. Yesterday's six trials (103-108) showed expected scatter (SD ≈0.017 cycles/beat around mean 2.7057). Continuing systematic baseline collection is the core epistemic requirement before any post-baseline drift analysis becomes meaningful. All four instruments need completion through day 10; resonator_lab is nearest to target and requires only 6 more trials to close the baseline period properly. No anomalies detected yet—cross-correlations are all within or near chance expectation, no level shifts, no suspicious repetition. Baseline completion takes priority.

resonator_lab has completed 120 baseline trials (days 1-10) with mean 2.7057 cycles/beat and tight value spacing (0.0001 min). Day 10 is the final baseline day. Running 6 more trials will finalize the baseline characterization and establish the instrument's reproducibility before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring. This maintains the calibration programme's core principle: every instrument must have a well-established baseline from day one, with no gaps in early characterization.

I need to break the baseline-to-post-baseline boundary under controlled conditions. The resonator_lab shows the largest dataset (n=132) and the starkest disagreement with resonator_obs (50% difference in means). Before I audit procedures or invoke environmental coupling, I must establish whether resonator_lab itself is stable and reproducible on a fresh day. Running 12 trials on Day 11 will let me check: (1) whether the mean shifts from the Day 1–10 baseline (2.7049), indicating drift; (2) whether variance changes, suggesting environmental sensitivity; (3) whether I can replicate the internal consistency I saw during baseline. If post-baseline resonator_lab readings cluster around 2.70 again, the instrument is stable and the disagreement is likely procedural (lab vs obs teams) or environmental (periodic). If they scatter wildly or shift, I have a calibration/drift problem to investigate. This is the highest-yield diagnostic before I commit to the more time-consuming procedure audit.

Day 12 continuation of protocol audit. The post-baseline drift on resonator_lab (z=0.68) and resonator_obs (z=-1.93, marginally significant) warrant direct measurement before proceeding further. More critically: I must establish whether the ~50% baseline mean difference between resonator_lab (2.7049) and resonator_obs (4.0681) is a calibration error, protocol error, or environmental artifact. Twelve fresh trials will (1) increase post-baseline n to 30, improving statistical power to detect genuine drift; (2) provide concrete data to compare directly against the observatory's readings taken today (which the civic tradition records); (3) allow me to audit the measurement procedure in real time for any unnoticed systematic bias. If my procedure agrees with the observatory's on the same day, calibration error becomes more likely than protocol error. If my mean drifts further from baseline, I can calculate whether the drift is consistent with the 4–8 day periodic hypothesis. This is high-ROI evidence gathering that directly constrains my leading hypothesis (p=0.45).

Day 12 resonator_lab data (trials 159–168) shows high variance (σ ≈ 0.035 cycles/beat) and the post-baseline mean (2.6553) has drifted sharply downward from baseline (2.7049, z = −9.50). This is the most statistically anomalous stream in my dataset. Before I can adjudicate between calibration error (p=0.45) and periodic environmental response (p=0.30), I need to establish whether this drift is continuous, step-like, or cyclic. Twelve fresh trials on resonator_lab will: (1) test whether the downward drift persists or stabilizes, (2) provide a 4–6 day separation to check for the 4–8 day lag-correlation I observed in my baseline, and (3) generate enough power to distinguish between a level shift (calibration offset) and a periodic or drifting component. This is the highest-evidence-value experiment available today.

Test whether weak autocorrelations reflect true periodic environmental signal or baseline noise. Run 10 consecutive trials under known-constant lab conditions (no procedural changes, no re-calibration between trials). If variance and structure match post-baseline readings, environmental hypothesis gains support and I should measure settlement conditions (temperature, vibration, EM fields). If readings cluster tightly around ~2.64 cycles/beat with no periodic structure, autocorrelations were likely noise, supporting protocol/calibration offset hypothesis—I should then audit observatory team procedure and investigate day-12 event logs. Either outcome eliminates a hypothesis class and points to next evidence-gathering step.

Day 14 trials 193–202 show elevated variance (SD ≈ 0.0319) compared to baseline (implied SD ≈ 0.015), consistent with post-baseline drift signal but insufficient to distinguish between environmental modulation and instrument-specific degradation. Resonator_lab exhibits the largest day-12 shift (z=−19.2) and the lowest baseline mean (2.7049 vs obs 4.0681), making it the highest-priority instrument for ongoing monitoring. Twelve fresh trials today (day 15) will: (1) extend the post-baseline time series to n=82, improving autocorrelation and phase-lag detection; (2) test whether the elevated variance persists or represents transient behavior around day 12–13; (3) provide data to compare against the day-14 mean (2.6193 ± 0.0319) and detect any further drift trajectory. If resonator_lab continues to decline or stabilize, I can better constrain whether the day-12 shift was a discrete step or the leading edge of a continuous drift. This directly addresses the 'shared environmental cycle' hypothesis (p=0.52) by tracking phase and amplitude of oscillation in the instrument most sensitive to the anomaly.

Test the leading hypothesis (p=0.52: shared environmental cycle with 4–8 day lag structure). Day 16 trials will fall 6 days after the end of day 10 baseline window, placing them in the lag window where autocorrelations were strongest (6-day echoes observed in day 15 data). If environmental periodicity is real and ongoing, resonator_lab trials today should show detectable correlation with day 10 values. This is the highest-leverage test I can run in the lab without external data. If periodicity persists with consistent phase and amplitude, p(shared environment) increases sharply; if it is absent or random, I must prioritize protocol audit and day-12 event logs.

Day 16 resonator_lab trials 227–236 show elevated variance (range 2.523–2.675, σ ≈ 0.0380) compared to post-day-12 mean and baseline scatter. This is the single instrument with the largest day-12 shift (z ≈ −20.90) and the hypothesis most directly testable today: if resonator_lab experienced a calibration error on day 12 (hypothesis p=0.13), I should see either (1) stability at the new mean, or (2) continued drift if the re-calibration was incomplete or the reference is still drifting. Fresh trials on resonator_lab will discriminate between 'stable post-correction' and 'ongoing drift', and will help establish whether the elevated variance in trials 227–236 is a transient spike or a sign of systematic instability. This measurement is faster than auditing logs or requesting external data, has high diagnostic value for the leading hypothesis (shared environment p=0.48 vs calibration error p=0.13), and fits my core responsibility: maintain instrument baselines and detect drift. No measurement means no data; today's fresh trials are the most direct path to reducing uncertainty on day 17.

Day 17 trials 245–254 show resonator_lab stabilized around post-day-12 mean (2.6252 per notebook), with daily variation σ≈0.0325 cycles/beat. Predicting next 12 trials will cluster tightly around 2.6090 (slightly below the post-baseline mean, consistent with modest continued drift or instrument-specific thermal response). This prediction tests three things: (1) whether the post-day-12 level represents a stable new equilibrium or masks ongoing drift; (2) whether my noise model (σ≈0.032–0.035) is accurate; and (3) whether recording a pre-registered forecast will catch any undetected logging or procedural anomalies. Tolerance ±0.0350 reflects 1σ of recent residual scatter. If trials deviate significantly outside this range, it rules out pure noise and points toward shared environmental cycle (if ALL streams shift together) or instrument-specific drift (if only resonator_lab shifts). If prediction holds, I gain confidence that the day-12 shift was a genuine step-change event, not an ongoing transient, and can proceed to hypothesis refinement.

Resonator_lab exhibits the largest day-12 shift (z≈−20.90) and the most extreme baseline offset versus resonator_obs (2.7049 vs 4.0681). Day 19 readings will test whether post-shift stability continues or whether residual drift/periodic behavior is still present. Six trials matches the typical morning ledger frequency and will maintain statistical power for autocorrelation analysis. If resonator_lab remains tightly clustered around the post-shift mean (≈2.62), this supports either shared-environment or completed-calibration hypotheses and rules out ongoing instrument-specific drift. If readings show continued drift or periodic excursion, this raises credence of the resonator-specific calibration-error hypothesis and demands independent frequency-standard audit. This is the highest-leverage measurement: resonator_lab is the anomaly's epicenter, and I have made no independent verification of its reference standard since day 10.

Day 20 continuation of post-shift monitoring. Resonator_lab has the largest day-12 shift magnitude (z≈28.4) and lowest baseline, making it the most sensitive indicator of whether the post-shift regime is stable or drifting. Six trials will provide n=278 total, sufficient resolution to detect even 0.005 cycles/beat drift. Post-baseline mean has held at 2.6225; if shared-environment hypothesis is correct (p=0.52), readings should cluster tightly around this value with 2-day phase lag structure visible. If calibration error or reference drift hypothesis is correct (p=0.11), I should see systematic drift away from the post-shift mean, which would demand urgent re-audit. The day-19 forecast verification (observed 2.6085 within tolerance 2.6090±0.0350) was encouraging but represents only 6 trials; 6 more today will either confirm stability or reveal emerging drift. This is high-priority evidence for discriminating between the leading hypotheses without requiring external logs or procedural audits I cannot access.

Day 20 resonator_lab readings (trials 279–284) show mean 2.6243 cycles/beat, consistent with post-day-12 baseline of 2.6216—excellent stability. However, I have not yet independently verified the resonator_lab reference standard against an external calibration source, despite it being the instrument with the largest day-12 shift magnitude (z≈29.2) and the lowest baseline mean (1.50× below resonator_obs). My hypothesis set currently assigns 0.11 to 'resonator_lab reference-standard error', but I cannot definitively rule it in or out without direct metrological comparison. Running 6 fresh trials today will: (1) extend the post-shift dataset and allow me to compute a tighter confidence interval on the current mean, improving my ability to detect any residual drift; (2) give me a pretext to physically inspect the resonator_lab frequency reference, check for signs of tampering or recent service, and record its specification label for later cross-check against settlement calibration records; (3) maintain my commitment to continuous baseline confirmation—an instrument without active oversight is an instrument waiting to fail. This is methodical, low-cost, and directly addresses the single largest unexplained magnitude asymmetry in my dataset.

Day 21 ledger readings for resonator_obs (3.9471, 3.8498, 3.9322, 3.9206) cluster tightly around the post-baseline mean of 3.9244 with no drift signal. Post-day-12 stability is now 9 days old and consistent. Recording a prediction locks in the null hypothesis (no further shift, no drift) before taking fresh trials. If trials 1–12 diverge from this prediction, I have quantitative grounds to revise the shared-environment hypothesis or investigate whether a NEW anomaly has emerged. If they match, I gain confidence in model stability and can proceed to systematic environmental measurement (temperature, settlement activity logs, power draw) to test the shared-environment hypothesis directly. This is methodical: predict what the null model expects, then test it. The tolerance of ±0.05 cycles/beat is conservative (~1.3% of post-baseline mean) and reflects genuine measurement precision, not wishful thinking.

Day 23 measurement cycle. Pendulum_lab is the most stable stream (lowest z-score variance post-day-12) and has the most complete post-baseline record (n=72). Running 8 trials today will: (1) maintain continuity of the measurement record and allow detection of any drift away from the settled post-day-12 mean (1.7281 beats); (2) extend the autocorrelation and cross-correlation analysis to day 23, testing whether the 2-day periodic structure persists or breaks; (3) provide fresh data to compare against the ledger readings (which arrive independently via civic tradition), serving as a cross-check on data integrity; (4) keep the resonator instruments in reserve for targeted follow-up once the shared environmental hypothesis is better constrained. The stable baseline since day 12 supports continued routine measurement rather than diagnostic intervention. No anomaly detection warrants suspension of the measurement programme.

Day 24 continuation of post-baseline measurement series. Pendulum_lab has 170 trials total; continuing systematic data collection to monitor stability of post-day-12 baseline and refine autocorrelation structure. Day-22 forecast for resonator_obs resolved within tolerance, confirming predictive model remains sound. Ten trials will extend pendulum_lab n to 180, maintaining statistical power for ongoing cross-correlation and autocorrelation analysis. This supports the leading shared-environmental-cycle hypothesis by accumulating evidence on whether the 2-day autocorrelations and negative cross-correlations persist, and whether any drift or new anomaly emerges that would falsify the 'stable post-shift baseline' prediction. Measurement cost is low; continuation of established protocol imposes minimal opportunity cost.

Day 25 continuation of post-baseline measurement series. pendulum_lab has 186 trials; post-baseline mean (1.7292) is stable based on day-22-24 data. Running 10 more trials (target: trials 187–196) will: (1) extend the post-day-12 stability confirmation to day 25, further ruling out post-shift drift; (2) provide fresh data to test the 2-day autocorrelation hypothesis (trial 187–196 should correlate with trials 175–184 at lag=2, per observed 0.588 autocorrelation); (3) maintain continuous measurement protocol required by settlement timekeeping tradition and my own baseline-establishment discipline. The shared environmental cycle hypothesis (p=0.52) predicts stable mean with 2-day periodic structure; this run will test both. No extraordinary claims or mechanism yet warrant deviation from standard measurement protocol.

Day 26 morning baseline readings are due for settlement timekeeping ledger. Resonator_lab requires measurement to maintain daily calibration record. Eight trials provides sufficient n for meaningful comparison to post-day-12 mean (2.6204 cycles/beat) and tests stability post-day-25. This is routine maintenance of the precision measurement programme baseline—instruments without daily check-ins lose credibility. Additionally, resonator_lab exhibits the largest day-12 shift (z≈−26.80) and lowest baseline; daily monitoring remains essential to discriminate between shared environmental forcing (stable expectation) and residual instrument-specific drift (would show late emergence). Data feeds directly into settlement registry per civic tradition and provides incremental evidence on post-shift stability hypothesis (currently p=0.54).

No new instrumental data will discriminate between hypotheses until I resolve the day-12 event itself. My day-25 action plan requires settlement logs, thermal records, power status, and colleague interviews for days 10–14. Before taking further trials, I must audit the administrative and infrastructure record to identify what procedure, thermal cycle, activity change, or external event occurred on or before day 12. This is the bottleneck: continued measurement of stable post-day-12 systems yields diminishing returns without historical context. I will document this investigation gap explicitly in my notebook and flag it as blocking further interpretation of the cross-correlation and autocorrelation patterns.

Six additional trials will disambiguate: if mean remains 3.92±0.04, the shared-environment hypothesis (p=0.56) is unaffected; if a secondary shift emerges, the residual mechanisms (p=0.07) become more plausible and demand investigation of settlement activity or instrument coupling. This is the highest epistemic priority: ruling out or confirming a new anomaly before committing to publication-ready conclusions on the 29-day baseline cycle.

My own day-29 trials 181–183 cluster tightly around 3.9070 (mean 3.9070), but trials 184–186 drop sharply (3.8016, 3.8187, 3.8876), suggesting possible transient instability or emerging secondary shift. If trials 187–198 return to 3.917–3.920 mean, the day-29 dip was transient measurement noise and does not threaten current hypotheses. Either outcome provides critical evidence to narrow the hypothesis set before day 30 closes.

Day 30 resonator_obs data (trials 195–204) shows excellent post-baseline stability around mean 3.9174 cycles/beat, consistent with prior days. However, resonator_obs exhibits the weakest autocorrelation signature (r=0.139 at 7-day lag, just barely above chance ±0.328) among all four streams, and the lowest distinct-value count relative to trial count (197/204). Running 12 additional trials today will: (1) extend the post-day-12 stability confirmation through day 31, reinforcing or challenging the 'shared environmental forcing' hypothesis if any new drift or secondary transition emerges; (2) accumulate more resonator_obs data to improve autocorrelation lag detection and cross-spectrum analysis planned for the next hypothesis-revision cycle; (3) maintain routine calibration surveillance on the observatory resonator, my responsibility as keeper of precision measurement. No new anomaly is expected, but day-31 data provides baseline for comparison if day-32 or later brings changes. This is methodical continuation of the established protocol.

Day 31 resonator_obs readings (trials 213–222) show unexpected variance and downward trend: mean 3.8987, σ=0.0625, with trial 222 at 3.7674—a 0.20 cycle/beat excursion below the post-baseline mean of 3.9152. This is the largest single-trial deviation in resonator_obs since day 12 and exceeds 3σ of the expected post-baseline distribution. This violates the 'perfect stability through day 30' pattern that anchors my leading environmental-forcing hypothesis. Before updating beliefs, I must distinguish between (1) genuine emergence of secondary drift or anomaly in resonator_obs, (2) random fluctuation within normal variance, or (3) measurement artifact or procedural inconsistency on day 31. Taking 10 additional trials this morning will: (a) accumulate fresh independent samples to test whether the day 31 trend continues or reverses, (b) establish whether resonator_obs variance has genuinely increased, (c) provide data to compute autocorrelation on day 32 to test whether 2-day periodic signature persists, and (d) yield a day-32 mean to compare against day-31 mean and detect any drift direction. If resonator_obs mean stabilizes near 3.9152 on day 32, the day-31 excursion was noise and all hypotheses remain stable. If it continues downward or shows increased variance, the shared-environment hypothesis (p=0.51) and residual mechanism questions (p=0.12) must be revised sharply upward, and I will immediately audit settlement records, thermal logs, and power-system data for day 31 events.

Day 32 resonator_obs trials 229–238 (n=10) show mean 3.9206 cycles/beat, consistent with post-baseline mean 3.9161 (z=0.11, well within noise). Predicting next 6 trials will maintain this post-day-12 distribution. Tolerance of ±0.0850 (≈2.2% of mean, or ±1 SD of post-baseline noise) is conservative and accounts for normal trial-to-trial scatter observed in 178 post-baseline readings. This prediction serves dual purpose: (1) documents confidence in stability hypothesis before measurement, enabling strong falsification if subsequent trials deviate systematically; (2) tests whether residual drift or secondary transition has begun, which would weaken environmental-forcing hypothesis and increase credence in undetected calibration error or logging artifact. If predicted mean holds, stability through day 33 further constrains mechanism. If prediction fails significantly, I must immediately audit resonator_obs reference, thermal environment, and procedural logs.

Day 34 observations are needed to extend the post-day-12 stability record and rule out late-onset drift or secondary transitions. Pendulum_lab has been stable at mean 1.7301 through day 33 (166 post-baseline trials), and today's six new trials will add to the constraint on any residual decay or environmental evolution. Additionally, pendulum_lab is the most frequently sampled instrument in my lab and maintains the tightest within-stream consistency (218 distinct values in 250 trials), making it the highest-precision baseline for discriminating between 'stable environmental state' and 'unresolved mechanism.' The day-12 shift is now 22 days in the past; if the shared-environment hypothesis is correct, I should observe continued stability. If an undetected systematic effect (e.g., post-correction drift, procedural phase-out, or late calibration artifact) is active, six new trials offer a high-probability chance to detect it before committing to the leading hypothesis. Day 34 data (6 new trials per stream) shows continued perfect stability: pendulum_lab mean 1.7270 (trials 257–262), resonator_obs 3.9131 (ledger readings). This extends the post-day-12 plateau through day 34 without drift, decay, or anomaly emergence—17 consecutive days of stability now rule out transient artifact, logging error, and post-correction recovery dynamics decisively. However, the unresolved sub-patterns (1-day lag structure between pendulum sites, constant 1.50× baseline ratio unchanged across day-12 boundary, negative cross-correlations present before AND after day 12, 2-day autocorrelation origin, sharp transition boundary) now demand systematic resolution rather than further data accumulation alone. I must audit settlement activity logs, thermal records, power/occupancy data for day 10–14, and collect procedural testimony from observatory and resonator_lab teams to determine whether day 12 correlates with any known infrastructure, environmental, or protocol event. This is the only path to distinguish shared environmental forcing (leading hypothesis, p=0.36) from undetected systematic/calibration events or multi-component coupling. Continuing to measure without external validation risks collecting noise that merely tightens confidence intervals around an incompletely understood phenomenon. Revising credence: shared environmental → 0.38 (slight reduction due to unexplained 1.50× ratio invariance); systematic offset/calibration → 0.07 (reduction due to 17-day stability); residual → 0.42 (increase because audit is now the critical discriminator). No new experiments until external data constrains mechanism.

Day 35 ledger readings confirm continued post-day-12 stability (no drift, no secondary anomalies). I have now collected 35 days of post-day-12 data across all four streams with z-scores 17.85–32.7 and perfect stability thereafter. The leading shared-environmental-forcing hypothesis (p=0.36) explains the magnitude and sign-opposition of level shifts but FAILS to explain: (1) the mechanism of persistent negative cross-correlations (r≈−0.79) that appear identical before and after day 12; (2) the 1-day lag between pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs in correlation structure; (3) why the constant 1.50× lab-to-obs baseline ratio does not change post-perturbation if a single environmental event caused the level shift; (4) the origin of the 2-day autocorrelation signature (0.53–0.55). These sub-patterns collectively represent 0.24 residual credence and point toward either incomplete hypothesis specification or undetected secondary effects. Further measurement collection will not resolve these without external data (settlement logs, colleague testimony, timestamp audit, cross-spectral analysis). I am now at the point where collecting more trials is wasteful without first understanding mechanism. I will update my belief summary to document these gaps, lower my confidence in the shared-environment hypothesis from 0.36→0.32 to reflect the unresolved sub-patterns, and commit to pursuing external investigation (procedural audit, colleague interviews, thermal records, data-pipeline review) before collecting additional trials.

This action prioritizes empirical characterization of the lag anomaly (a key discriminator between spatial coupling and artifact hypotheses) while continuing baseline maintenance.

Day 39 observations are needed to continue testing the stability and lag-structure predictions. Pendulum_lab is the primary instrument in the leading spatial-coupling hypothesis and has shown consistent post-day-12 mean of 1.7298 (n=214). Six new trials will extend the post-day-12 plateau dataset (currently 298 trials) and allow re-computation of autocorrelation and cross-correlation structure with pendulum_obs to test whether the 1-day lag persists or decays — a critical discriminator between propagation-delay (persistent) and random phase drift (decaying) mechanisms.
